newsitem.title: USA: Leave decimal stock quotes to U.S. markets - D'Amato.
newsitem.headline: Leave decimal stock quotes to U.S. markets - D'Amato.

text.p: Senator Alfonse D'Amato said Wednesday Congress should not force U.S. stock markets to trade securities in decimals instead of fractions.
D'Amato, chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, said he favors decimal quotations, but sees market forces bringing about the change.

"Market competition and market forces are bringing this desirable result about and Congress should not interfere," the New York Republican said in a statement. Trading in decimals will "ultimately benefit consumers," he added.

D'Amato's comments come as a measure introduced in the House of Representatives cleared its first hurdle last month. The bill would require the Securities and Exchange Commission to map out a plan to shift trades in U.S. markets to decimals from fractions.

Most stocks are traded in eigths or sixteenths of a dollar, so the smallest trading increment is either 12.5 cents or 6.25 cents, respectively. Switching to decimals, could, in theory, allow these spreads to shrink to as little as one cent.

D'Amato's oppostion to such a move is consistent with the views of other New York lawmakers, including Democratic Rep. Thomas Manton and Republican Rep. Rick Lazio, both members of House Commerce Committee's finance subcommittee.
They echoed the concerns of the securities industry, which has maintained that market forces, not Congress, should drive the trend towards trading in decimals.

The bill cleared the finance subcommittee last month, but it is unclear when it will be considered by the full Commerce Committee. Chairman Thomas Bliley, Republican of Virginia, has said he supports the measure.
SEC chairman Arthur Levitt has not fully endorsed the measure, which was introduced by Ohio Republican Michael Oxley and Massachusetts Democrat Edward Markey.
Levitt said a move to decimal trading is inevitable, but warned that "implementation issues" could be tricky.
Already several exchanges have decided to allow trading in smaller fractions, one thirty-second and one sixteenth, which should allow traders to gain some savings from tighter spreads.
